title: Empty the tanks into the backwardation
trade: Sell 1 Mbbl of WTI from Cushing tanks for December, buy February WTI to refill
why: WTI is backwardated by about 1 $/bbl a month, so the market pays to release barrels now.
Hormuz has been shut since March. PortWatch counted 27 transits in the week to 8 November, against 527 a year earlier.
US crude stocks rose 9 Mbbl in the week to 6 November (API), so the refill should not be short.
hedge: The February futures are the hedge, swapped for physical (EFP) at refill. Tank rent and financing saved come on top if the tank can be sublet.
risks: Cushing physical trades over futures by February.
A refinery client needs the barrels before the refill arrives.

good.case: refill at a discount after more stock builds

bad.case: refill at a premium or buy back early

title: Sell diesel prompt, buy it back in February
trade: Sell 37 kt of ULSD from New York Harbor tanks for December, buy February NYMEX ULSD to refill
why: The distillate curve is the steepest on the board, about 2% a month in New York Harbor.
Russian refining is down about 30% since late October after drone strikes.
Hormuz and the Red Sea cut Middle East and Indian diesel flows to Europe.
hedge: February NYMEX ULSD futures, rolled into physical by EFP at refill.
risks: New York barges trade over futures at refill.
A January squeeze forces an early buy-back.

good.case: refill at a discount as imports arrive

bad.case: buy back early in a January squeeze

title: Send a December US cargo to Asia instead of Europe
trade: Buy a FOB Sabine Pass cargo at its European netback, sell DES Japan or Korea on December JKM
why: A spot US cargo is priced off Europe, its usual outlet. 57% of US exports went there in September.
December JKM trades about 2.6 $/MMBtu over TTF, and January JKM is 2.66 $/MMBtu below December.
Panama delivers in about 22 days, so the cargo still prices December.
hedge: At loading, sell December JKM and buy December TTF for the cargo size.
risks: Arrival slips into January and the cargo loses 2.66 $/MMBtu on the curve.
A European cold spell closes the JKM − TTF gap.
Sold DES, the boil-off and any Panama delay are the seller's.

good.case: JKM − TTF widens by 2 on Asian tenders

title: South African coal goes east, not to Europe
trade: Buy 150 kt FOB Richards Bay on API4, sell CFR Japan at Newcastle plus freight
why: Europe is shut. API2 − API4 is about 9 $/t against 24 $/t of Capesize freight to Rotterdam.
Japan pays Newcastle plus the Panamax freight from Australia, which leaves room for a Capesize from Richards Bay.
API4 is backwardated, with November at 127 and December at 123 $/t, so December loading buys cheaper.
hedge: Buy API4 swaps against the purchase and sell NEWC swaps against the sale. Fix the Capesize at today's 5TC.
risks: Each +10k $/day on the Capesize costs about 3.9 $/t.
Newcastle weakens if Chinese domestic output recovers.
Sold CFR, the freight is the seller's risk from the day the price is agreed.

title: European coil still lands under US prices after the tariff
trade: Buy 30 kt of coil ex-works in the Ruhr, sell duty paid in Houston on a CME-linked price
why: US Midwest coil is about 1,351 $/st. After 30 $/t to reach the ship, 45 $/t of freight and the 50% tariff, European coil still lands below it.
The EU's new steel regime, with a 50% out-of-quota duty since 1 July, shut Chinese coil out of Europe. European mills have tonnes to place.
The CME curve is in contango, with January near 1,430 $/st, so a sale priced on arrival pays more than today.
hedge: Sell CME HRC futures for the arrival month when the purchase is fixed.
risks: US mills cut prices before the cargo lands.
Sold duty paid, the tariff is the seller's. A rate change before customs clearance hits the margin.
A US anti-dumping case on European flat steel.

good.case: sale priced on the January contract

bad.case: US prices fall about 140 $/st before arrival

title: Cathodes to the US, a cheap option on the copper tariff
trade: Take 5 kt of copper out of an LME warehouse in Rotterdam, clear it through US customs and hold it against COMEX
why: COMEX − LME is about +65 $/t, so the market prices almost no tariff on refined copper.
Commerce recommended 15% on refined copper from 1 January 2027. The White House has not decided.
Getting the metal there costs about 175 $/t and the spread pays back 65, so the option costs about 110 $/t.
hedge: Sell COMEX March and buy LME 3-month against the shipment. Only the spread stays open.
risks: No tariff, and the spread can go to a discount while the carry is lost.
The metal must clear customs before the tariff starts, or the duty lands on the trader.
A queue at LME Rotterdam delays the load-out past the decision.

bad.case: no decision, COMEX at a discount
